openers.time-risk-and-discounting: A dollar today is not the same as a dollar next year. Rising prices make each unit of money buy less, borrowers pay lenders extra for the use of their money, and most people simply value getting something sooner rather than later. This chapter builds the tools for comparing money across time, ending with the worth today of payments still to come. It also takes on uncertainty, the many situations where information is imperfect or unknown, and the idea of averaging possible outcomes by how likely each one is. Together these tools shape how people judge any choice whose costs and benefits are spread across years.

nature-econ-801.title: Inflation: why money buys a little less each year
nature-econ-801.text: Since the Great Depression of the 1930s, prices have generally risen every year. That steady climb is inflation: a rise in the average price of goods and services measured in money, so that each unit of money buys less. It describes the general trend of prices, not a change in any single price. Economists measure it with a {{ref:nature-econ-832}}, usually one that tracks consumer prices, and the inflation rate is the yearly percentage change in that measure. The opposite, a fall in the general price level, is called deflation. Causes include growth in the amount of money in circulation, demand shocks, supply shocks such as energy crises, interest-rate cuts and changing expectations. High or unpredictable inflation does real harm. It makes long-term planning hard, and doubt about what money will be worth later discourages people from putting money aside and firms from building for the future. It also shifts buying power away from people living on fixed payments, such as pensioners whose pensions are not indexed to prices. Most economists today favor a low and steady inflation rate, a task usually given to a {{ref:nature-econ-561}}.

nature-econ-772.title: Uncertainty: deciding without knowing
nature-econ-772.text: Predictions of the future, measurements already taken and the plain unknown all share one trait. Each carries uncertainty, which describes any situation where information is imperfect or unknown. It matters most when someone has to make a decision. Uncertainty arises in environments that are partly observable, random, complex or changing, and from simple ignorance. More precisely, it is a state of limited knowledge in which the possible future states, their probabilities or their values cannot all be fully described. That limits what can be measured. Uncertainty can be measured only when it is treated as risk, by assigning a probability to each possible outcome. One practical response is {{ref:nature-nbs-146}}, a step-by-step way of deciding under uncertainty that aims to shrink it over time through monitoring.

nature-econ-756.title: Expected value: the average of what might happen
nature-econ-756.text: In the mid-17th century, a puzzle called the problem of points asked how to split the stakes fairly when a game ends early. Pascal and Fermat solved it on a simple principle: a future gain is worth an amount proportional to the chance of getting it. From that came expected value, the average of an uncertain quantity's possible values, each weighted by how likely it is. A fair six-sided die makes it concrete. Each face from 1 to 6 has probability 1/6, so the expected value is 3.5, a number the die can never show. When all outcomes are equally likely, the expected value is simply the ordinary average. It can also be read as the long-run average from repeating the same random experiment many times, as the law of large numbers shows. Christiaan Huygens published the first treatise on it in 1657, often seen as the first foundation of probability theory. The usual notation, E(X), uses a letter that goes back to W. A. Whitworth in 1901. In {{ref:nature-econ-787}}, a person choosing with incomplete information is often assumed to maximize the expected value of their utility.

nature-econ-797.title: Expected utility: weighing outcomes by what they mean to you
nature-econ-797.text: An extra sum of money is worth less to a rich person than to a poor one. Bernoulli's version of that insight was the first formal statement of marginal utility, and it grew into the expected utility hypothesis. The hypothesis holds that people choose between risky options by comparing the probability-weighted average of the utility of each outcome. Expected utility is the sum over outcomes of each payoff's utility times its probability. The shape of the utility curve captures a person's attitude to risk. It is a straight line for someone risk-neutral, convex, bending upward, for a risk-seeker, and concave, bending downward, for someone who shuns risk. Von Neumann and Morgenstern defined a rational decision-maker by four axioms: completeness, transitivity, independence and continuity. The hypothesis is a foundational assumption of mathematical economics about decisions under uncertainty, and rational choice theory builds on it. Yet psychologists have found systematic violations. Researchers have produced broader theories, such as {{ref:nature-econ-067}}, to account for them. These departures are called irrational because they depend on how a problem is presented, not on its costs, rewards or probabilities.

nature-econ-811.title: Interest: the price of waiting for your money
nature-econ-811.text: Sumerian documents from 3000 BC show systematic lending of grain and metals, and interest seems to have been well established even then. Interest is the extra money a borrower pays a lender, on top of repaying the amount borrowed, at a set rate. A bank customer usually pays interest to borrow, paying back more than was lent. The same customer earns interest on money deposited, withdrawing more than was put in. Unlike a dividend, which a company shares out from profit, interest is paid at a rate fixed beforehand. Why pay it at all? In the sixteenth century Martín de Azpilcueta argued that a good now is better than the same good later. Interest pays the lender for giving up spending in the meantime. Another explanation for rates usually staying above zero is scarcity: loanable funds are limited. In economics the {{ref:nature-econ-757}} is the price of credit and acts as the {{ref:nature-econ-784}}. Interest even shaped mathematics. Jacob Bernoulli is thought to have discovered the constant e by studying what happens as interest is compounded more and more often.

nature-econ-757.title: Interest rates: the cost of money now instead of later
nature-econ-757.text: Firms borrow from banks expecting the borrowed capital to earn a return greater than the cost of the loan. That cost is set by the interest rate: the interest charged or paid each period, expressed as a share of the amount lent, deposited or borrowed. Rates are normally quoted per year. Total interest depends on the rate together with the principal, the sum originally lent, and on how often interest compounds and for how long. At heart, a rate reflects a borrower's willingness to pay for money now rather than money in the future. When rates change, the opportunity cost of funding new projects rises or falls for firms. Risk matters too. Riskier choices such as shares and high-risk 'junk' debt normally have to promise higher returns than safer government debt. Banks themselves live on the spread, the lending rate minus the deposit rate, which covers their operating costs.

nature-econ-831.title: Real versus nominal: counting money or counting what it buys
nature-econ-831.text: A pay rise looks good on paper, but what matters is what the wage will buy. A nominal value is measured in plain money amounts. A real value is measured by the goods and services that money can actually buy, so it allows for inflation and reflects purchasing power. To find it, divide the nominal value by the growth factor of a {{ref:nature-econ-832}}, giving values in, for example, constant 1992 dollars. Real wages work this way: the after-tax nominal wage divided by the growth factor of consumer prices. In one example the real wage rose 20 percent, so an hour's wage bought 20% more goods in year 2 than in year 1. The same logic applies to whole economies. Real GDP removes inflation from growth figures to show how much an economy actually grows, while nominal GDP includes inflation and is higher. Output from different regions can be compared by repricing their goods at common or average prices.

nature-econ-839.title: Time preference: why sooner beats later
nature-econ-839.text: Would you take $100 today or $110 in a month? Taking the $100 implies an annual {{ref:nature-econ-746}} of at least 10%. That pull toward the present is time preference: how much more a person values getting something sooner rather than later. The higher it is, the more future returns or costs are discounted, or shrunk in value today. Economists capture it with a {{ref:nature-econ-791}}, and the main models are exponential, hyperbolic and quasi-hyperbolic. John Rae began the study. He argued that nations differ in prosperity because they differ in how much they put aside, driven by willingness to delay gratification. In Irving Fisher's neoclassical theory, the rate of time preference underlies the real rate of interest. The idea now sits at the center of climate policy. Thomas Schelling framed {{ref:nature-hist-007}} as a problem of sharing welfare between present and future generations. The {{ref:nature-clim-268}} set δ = .1%, η = 1 and g = 1.3%, giving a 1.4% rate. The economist {{ref:nature-hist-050}} objected that this near-zero time preference drove its conclusions. Experts still disagree about the right rate for climate decisions, and the rates countries reveal in their environmental choices span 1%-10%.

nature-econ-769.title: Why a dollar today beats a dollar tomorrow
nature-econ-769.text: A dollar today is worth more than a dollar in the future, because money held today can be invested to earn a return. This is the time value of money: receiving a sum now is generally better than receiving the same sum later. It is one reason interest exists, since interest compensates a depositor or lender for losing the use of their money. It also shapes the opportunity cost of spending money rather than putting it to work. The method compares cash flows at different dates by converting them all to one valuation date, often called time 0. An amount PV invested at rate i grows to PV(1 + i)^n after n periods. Running the formula backwards finds the {{ref:nature-econ-762}}. That formula is the central one. The others, such as the one for an {{ref:nature-econ-779}}, are built from it. Business has used {{ref:nature-econ-781}} since the Middle Ages, and pricing streams of regular payments was a key setting for developing present-value methods. Today {{ref:nature-val-001}} adjusts all costs and benefits for the time value of money, expressing them as a {{ref:nature-val-014}}.

nature-econ-762.title: Present value: what future money is worth today
nature-econ-762.text: A $100 note payable in one year, paying no interest along the way, sells today for $80. That $80 is its present value: what a stream of expected future payments is worth as of today. Present value usually sits below what the money will be worth later, because money held now can earn interest. Put simply, a dollar today is worth more than a dollar tomorrow, since today's dollar can be invested and earn a day's interest. Working out what money today will be worth later is called capitalization; the reverse, valuing future money today, is {{ref:nature-econ-745}}. The usual model uses {{ref:nature-econ-781}}, and (1 + i) to the power −n is called the present value factor. The {{ref:nature-val-014}} of a stream of cash flows discounts each flow to the present and adds them up. The rate chosen depends on risk. Riskless projects use a risk-free interest rate, while risky ones add a {{ref:nature-econ-836}} judged from projects with similar risks. When both the timing and size of payments are uncertain, an expected present value approach weighs several scenarios by their probabilities.

nature-econ-745.title: Discounting: paying to put off a payment
nature-econ-745.text: Most people prefer money now to money later, because of mortality, impatience and salience effects, the pull of what is vivid and close at hand. Discounting builds that preference into a deal. Someone who owes money pays a charge for the right to delay the payment for a set time. The discount is the gap between what is owed today and the larger amount that must be paid later to settle the debt. Why should a delay cost anything? A payment made in the future is worth less than the same payment today, because money in hand now could be banked to earn interest. The debtor who delays is in effect compensating the creditor for what the money could have earned meanwhile. Most models assume the discount yield equals the return the money could earn elsewhere, at similar risk, over the same period. Discounting also runs the other way, turning a future payment into its present value, also called its discounted value. Either way it rests on the time value of money: the same payment is worth one amount in the future and another today.

nature-econ-787.title: Decision theory: the logic of choosing under uncertainty
nature-econ-787.text: Should a windfall be spent now or saved for a pension? Decision theory, also called the theory of rational choice, uses expected utility and probability to model how people would act rationally under uncertainty. Choice under uncertainty is its heart, and it also covers choices whose outcomes arrive at different times. It is mainly prescriptive: it identifies the best decisions for a rational agent rather than describing how people actually choose. Its roots lie in 17th-century probability theory from Pascal and Fermat, refined by Huygens. Daniel Bernoulli introduced expected utility in the 18th century, and von Neumann and Morgenstern formalized it in the 1940s. Then the cracks appeared. Allais and Ellsberg showed systematic departures from expected-utility maximization. Kahneman and Tversky's {{ref:nature-econ-067}} renewed empirical study. They found that losses loom larger than gains and that people focus on changes rather than levels. Their probability estimates are biased by anchoring, the pull of a starting number.

nature-econ-781.title: Compound interest: earning interest on interest
nature-econ-781.text: Put $1,000 in an account at 5% a year. After one year it holds $1,050; after two, $1,102.50, because the second year's interest is paid on the new total. That is compound interest: interest earned both on the original sum and on interest already added to it. It differs from {{ref:nature-econ-812}}, where past interest is not added to the principal. Compounding can happen yearly, monthly, daily, continuously, or not at all until the loan matures. At a constant rate it makes capital grow exponentially, by the same proportion each period. Luca Pacioli's rule from 1494 says the years for money to double is roughly 72 divided by the interest rate. Not everyone admired the arithmetic. Under Roman law, lenders charging compound interest were condemned as the worst kind of usury, or extortionate lending. The ecologist {{ref:nature-hist-052}} argued that any economy based on long-term compound interest must fail, since growth of that kind is impossible on a finite planet.

nature-econ-844.title: Von Neumann and Morgenstern: rational choice as expected utility
nature-econ-844.text: In 1947 John von Neumann and Oskar Morgenstern proved a far-reaching result. Anyone whose preferences meet four axioms acts as if maximizing expected utility. The axioms are completeness, transitivity, continuity and independence. Choices are framed as lotteries: sets of outcomes, each with a probability, the probabilities summing to one. The theorem shows that rational choice under uncertainty amounts to maximizing the expected value of some utility function. It claims only that such a function exists, not that people consciously maximize it. A dislike of risk comes built in, since utility need not rise in step with money. Two limits stand out. Its utilities cannot be compared or added across people, so a group's 'total' or 'average' utility means nothing without extra assumptions. And lab experiments such as the Allais paradox show that expected utility predicts imperfectly. Most broader theories drop or relax the independence axiom.

nature-econ-818.title: Intertemporal choice: trading today against tomorrow
nature-econ-818.text: Whatever is consumed today cannot be consumed in the future. Intertemporal choice studies how people value payoffs that arrive at different times, usually simplified to now versus some future date. John Rae introduced the idea in 1834; Eugen von Böhm-Bawerk in 1889 and Irving Fisher in 1930 developed the model further. Diminishing marginal utility is a key tool for analyzing such choices, along with choice under uncertainty and social welfare. The stakes reach energy use. Uncertain fuel prices, and the heavy discounting many people apply to future running costs, make spending on energy efficiency look riskier to many decision makers.

nature-econ-824.title: Minimax: choosing the least bad worst case
nature-econ-824.text: A cautious chooser can set probabilities aside and ask a single question: what is the worst that could happen? Minimax is the decision rule that picks the option whose worst possible outcome is least bad. Framed in terms of gains it is called maximin, maximizing the minimum gain. A player's maximin value is the most they can be sure of getting without knowing what the other players will do. The rule was first formulated for games in which one player's gain is the other's loss, the {{ref:nature-econ-742}}, and later extended to general decisions under uncertainty. In two-player games of that kind the minimax solution is the same as the {{ref:nature-econ-718}}. Minimax values are also central to the theory of games played over and over, including the {{ref:nature-econ-717}}. The rule suits cases without good probability models, but it can overweight very unlikely, costly events.

nature-econ-773.title: Risk: uncertainty with numbers attached
nature-econ-773.text: Not knowing whether it will rain tomorrow is uncertainty. Giving rain a probability, say from a weather forecast, turns it into risk. Risk is uncertainty that has been quantified: the possible outcomes have known probabilities, and some of them involve losses. Suppose a business event loses $100,000 if it rains, and rain has a 10% chance. The risk is a 10% chance of losing $100,000. The expected opportunity loss multiplies the chance of loss by its size, here $10,000. That figure suits only a risk-neutral decision-maker, one who cares about the average alone. Most people would pay a premium to avoid the loss, so insurers charge more than the expected loss. Risk also differs from variability. Risk concerns one uncertain value still to come; variability is the spread of many observed values.

nature-econ-805.title: Insurance: a small sure cost against a large uncertain one
nature-econ-805.text: Chinese merchants once split their cargo across many boats, so that one capsizing lost little. Chinese and Indian traders spread risk this way as early as the 3rd and 2nd millennia BC. Insurance does the same job today. It is protection from financial loss: for a fee, one party promises to pay another if a particular loss, damage or injury happens. The buyer accepts a certain, known and fairly small loss, the premium, in exchange for the insurer's promise to pay if a covered loss occurs. A deductible, or excess, is the amount the insured must pay out of pocket before the insurer pays a claim. Insurance moves the financial burden of a chance event to a bigger entity. It does not lower the chance that the event happens. What separates it from gambling is the need for an insurable interest, a real stake in the loss. In the United States, economists and consumer advocates generally see insurance as worthwhile for rare, catastrophic losses but not for likely, small ones. It can help households and societies prepare for and soften catastrophes. It can also raise fraud and careless behavior, the moral hazard met earlier.

nature-econ-765.title: Risk aversion: why a sure thing often wins
nature-econ-765.text: Offer someone a sure $50 or a coin flip for $100 or nothing. A risk-averse person takes the sure thing, and would even accept a sure amount below $50, such as $40. Risk aversion is this tendency to prefer a more certain outcome to a riskier one, even when the risky option pays the same or more on average. A risk-neutral person is indifferent between the bet and a sure $50. A risk-loving person takes the bet even against a sure $60. The same instinct leads an investor to choose a bank account with a low guaranteed rate over shares that could pay more but might lose value. Economists measure the attitude with the certainty equivalent, the smallest sure amount a person would accept instead of a gamble. The gap between a gamble's expected value and its certainty equivalent is the {{ref:nature-econ-836}}, positive for the risk-averse. In expected utility theory, a person is risk-averse exactly when their utility function is concave, bending downward. On average, higher earners are less risk-averse than lower earners.

nature-econ-836.title: The risk premium: the extra return that pays for risk
nature-econ-836.text: An investor can buy risk-free government debt paying 3%. To choose a risky share instead, she might demand 8%. The 5% gap is her risk premium: the extra return demanded for accepting more risk, generally the expected risky return minus the risk-free return. The more risk averse a person or firm, the larger the premium they will pay to avoid a risk, and it usually falls as people grow richer. Premiums swell during economic downturns and periods of heightened uncertainty. For a {{ref:nature-mkt-065}} the risk premium is called the credit spread, the extra yield over risk-free government debt. Schroeder estimated share-market risk premiums of 4.83 to 7.75 percent in the UK and EU, mostly between 6.3 and 7.2 percent. The idea reaches farms and ecosystems too. In some models, the value of keeping options open by spending on quarantine or management of an {{ref:nature-eco-026}} is a risk premium. When a wheat variety resistant to several diseases was released in 2000, it sharply cut the risk premium farmers bore against the crop disease Fusarium head blight.

nature-econ-784.title: Cost of capital: the bar every project must clear
nature-econ-784.text: Every new project a company considers has to clear a bar. That bar is the cost of capital: what a company pays for its funds, both borrowed and from shareholders, or the return investors require for providing them. It is the minimum return investors expect, so a project is worthwhile only if its expected return exceeds it. It also equals what the money could earn in the best alternative of similar risk, the opportunity cost of capital. Finding it means estimating both the cost of debt and the {{ref:nature-econ-786}}, and both must look forward to expected future risk and return. Financial calculations usually set the {{ref:nature-econ-746}} equal to the cost of capital. One caution applies. For projects outside a firm's main business, its usual cost of capital may be the wrong yardstick, since the risks differ.
